Bekah
BEK-ah
n. (Hebrew)
Hebrew beqa‘, “a half,” from bāqa‘ (to split, divide); a half-shekel weight, the standard amount for the half-shekel atonement-tax of Exodus 30:11-16.

📖 Biblical Definition

The bekah is the Hebrew half-shekel weight (the word means literally a half), the standard amount specified for the atonement-tax every adult Israelite male paid for the support of the tabernacle’s service. Exodus 30:11-16 prescribes the doctrine: when thou takest the sum of the children of Israel after their number, then shall they give every man a ransom for his soul unto the LORD, when thou numberest them; that there be no plague among them, when thou numberest them. This they shall give, every one that passeth among them that are numbered, half a shekel after the shekel of the sanctuary: (a shekel is twenty gerahs:) an half shekel shall be the offering of the LORD. Every one that passeth among them that are numbered, from twenty years old and above, shall give an offering unto the LORD. The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less than half a shekel, when they give an offering unto the LORD, to make an atonement for your souls. The detail of the doctrine is theologically substantive. First, the equality of the atonement-payment: the rich and poor pay the same exact amount—the half-shekel ransom is the same for every soul, because every soul’s value before God is the same, and the atonement-substitute is not measured by the offerer’s means but by the soul’s objective worth. Second, the universal obligation: every adult male above twenty years pays; no one is exempt; the principle of universal liability for atonement is built into the very census-procedure. Third, the soul-language: the payment is explicitly a ransom for his soul and to make an atonement for your souls; the bekah is not generic tax-revenue but specifically substitutionary-atonement money. Fourth, the plague-prevention: the payment that there be no plague among them, when thou numberest them recalls David’s later sin of numbering Israel without the atonement-payment (2 Sam 24; 1 Chr 21), which resulted in the plague that David then atoned for by buying Araunah’s threshingfloor (the site of the future temple). Fifth, the temple-service support: the half-shekel funded the ongoing service of the tabernacle (and later the temple), so that the atonement-payment of each Israelite was the financial sustenance of the sanctuary’s worship. Sixth, the typological substance. The half-shekel atonement-tax prefigured the full ransom Christ would pay for every soul: not the half-shekel of equal token-payment but the precious blood of the Lamb without blemish, paid as the once-for-all ransom that no soul could pay for itself and that perfectly redeems every soul for whom it was offered. The bekah is therefore not numismatic curiosity but the precise OT figure of the substitutionary atonement Christ Himself accomplished.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

(Hebrew term.) BEKAH: a half-shekel weight; the standard amount specified in Ex 30:11-16 for the atonement-tax every adult Israelite male paid for the support of the tabernacle’s service; explicitly named as a ransom for his soul and prefiguring the full ransom Christ would pay for every soul.

BEKAH, n. — (Hebrew weight.) A half-shekel weight; the half-shekel atonement-tax of Ex 30:11-16, paid by every adult Israelite male as a ransom for his soul.

RANSOM, n. — The money or price paid for the redemption of a prisoner or slave, or for procuring the release of a forfeit; in scripture, the price of redemption for the soul, paid in OT type as the half-shekel and in substantive reality as the precious blood of Christ (1 Pet 1:18-19).

📖 Key Scripture

Exodus 30:13 — "This they shall give, every one that passeth among them that are numbered, half a shekel after the shekel of the sanctuary: (a shekel is twenty gerahs:) an half shekel shall be the offering of the LORD."

Exodus 30:15 — "The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less than half a shekel, when they give an offering unto the LORD, to make an atonement for your souls."

1 Peter 1:18-19 — "Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers; But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot."

Genesis 24:22 — "And it came to pass, as the camels had done drinking, that the man took a golden earring of half a shekel weight..."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The bekah half-shekel atonement-tax is corrupted chiefly by the general loss of OT-cultic typology that has dropped its explicit Christological substance (the ransom-for-the-soul that prefigured Christ’s full ransom of every soul)—and by the inverse error of treating the equal half-shekel payment as a generic principle of equal taxation without the substantive substitutionary-atonement theology that grounds it.

expand to see more

The general loss of OT-cultic typology has dropped the bekah half-shekel atonement-tax from contemporary preaching as obscure cultic detail without operative theological substance. Yet the substance is significant. The half-shekel payment is explicitly named as a ransom for his soul; the equality of rich-and-poor payment teaches that the soul’s atonement-value is uniform; the universal obligation teaches that every soul requires atonement; the plague-prevention rationale grounds the doctrine in the LORD’s holiness against numbered souls without atonement. And the typological substance is direct: the half-shekel prefigured the full ransom Christ would pay for every soul, the precious blood of the Lamb without blemish that no human payment could substitute and that perfectly redeems every soul for whom it was offered. The recovery is the recovery of the typological reading: 1 Peter 1:18-19 is the apostolic application of the OT ransom-language, and the bekah is one of its most precise typological anchors.

The opposite corruption is the treatment of the equal half-shekel payment as a generic principle of equal-tax-rates without the substantive substitutionary-atonement theology. Some readings have taken Ex 30:15 (the rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less) as authorizing flat-tax political theory or as a generic principle of equal-treatment-before-God in financial matters. The text’s actual structure is more specific. The equality is grounded not in a generic flat-tax principle but in the substitutionary-atonement reality: the soul-value is uniform; the atonement-substitute is the same for every soul; the half-shekel is not generic taxation but specifically ransom-payment. Read the equality off from the atonement-doctrine, not the atonement-doctrine off from a generic equality-of-taxation principle. The bekah’s substantive doctrine is the substitutionary atonement; the equality-of-payment is a feature of that doctrine, not the doctrine itself. Recover both ends. Refuse the loss of OT-cultic typology that drops the doctrine altogether, and refuse the over-extension that treats the bekah’s equality-of-payment as a generic political principle. The biblical bekah teaches the universal need for atonement, the uniform value of every soul before God, and the typological anticipation of the full ransom Christ would pay—the substantive substitutionary-atonement doctrine that grounds the gospel itself.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew beqa‘ (a half), from bāqa‘ (to split); a half-shekel weight, the standard amount for the atonement-tax of Ex 30:11-16, paid equally by every adult Israelite male as a ransom for his soul, prefiguring the full ransom Christ would pay for every soul (1 Pet 1:18-19).

expand to see more

Hebrew beqa‘ (H1235) — a half, half-shekel (Gen 24:22; Ex 38:26).

Hebrew bāqa‘ (H1234) — to split, divide (the verb behind the noun).

Hebrew sheqel ha-qōdesh — shekel of the sanctuary (the standard against which the half-shekel was measured; Ex 30:13).

Greek lutron (G3083) — ransom (the NT counterpart; Matt 20:28; 1 Tim 2:6).
